research_rationale: EO 1547 (June 19, 1912, William H. Taft), read in full in the held ProQuest replica scan (archival_replica_scan_pending_codebook, acceptable_as_original false) and checked against the page image I rendered from the held PDF (sha256 2e446a81...; one page; printed number 'No. 1547', date 'June 19, 1912', signature 'Wm H Taft'). The OCR layer is complete; its errors ('I19' for 19, a stray apostrophe after 'hereby', '[No. 1547-.1') do not affect the operative words. Single operative command: under section 2 of the act of June 19, 1912 limiting the hours of daily service of laborers and mechanics on federal work (the 1912 eight-hour act), the act's provisions and stipulations 'are hereby waived, until January first, nineteen hundred and fifteen, as to any contract or contracts entered into in connection with the construction of the Isthmian Canal.' First end: by its own terms on 1915-01-01. Under the owner's 2026-10-21 ruling the 'until' date is inclusive, so the waiver runs through the end of January 1, 1915; the alternative exclusive reading is that it stopped when that day began, leaving December 31, 1914 as its last day. Authority check: no held source shows section 2 of the 1912 act repealed or amended before 1915; the held text of EO 2663 (1917, jobs/wikisource-texts/output/texts/EO_2663.txt) invokes section 2 of the same act (37 Stat. 137), which corroborates that the authority still existed after this order's end. The act's own effective-date clause is not held; it does not affect the end. The order states its own date, so its end does not depend on when the canal construction contracts were completed.
savings_reason: Contracts entered into while the waiver ran could lawfully omit the eight-hour stipulations, and work done under them was lawful. Where such a contract continued after January 1, 1915, its terms stood as made; that is an accrued effect of a contract formed under the waiver, carried by the contract and the 1912 act, and it does not keep the order operative, because the order commands nothing after its stated date. Pay for hours worked flows from the contracts and statute, not from the order. No held source shows any contract affected after 1915; this residual is a disclosed qualification, not a finding.
earlier_end_check: No earlier end is held. Candidates considered and not shown to extinguish the waiver: the Panama Canal Act of August 24, 1912 and EO 1885 (January 27, 1914, permanent organization of the Panama Canal) with EO 1888 (February 2, 1914, conditions of employment). The waiver attaches to contracts for canal construction, not to the Isthmian Canal Commission, and neither order's held summary or text names EO 1547 or the 1912 act's waiver; under the owner's rule a later general instrument ends a command only if something shows it extinguished that command, and nothing held does. The Panama Canal Act's text is not held. No extension: census titles, the WPA 1944 numbered list and the full text of all 2,750 ProQuest scan texts were searched on 2026-10-28 for Isthmian or Panama Canal orders touching eight-hour or hours-of-labor rules between 1912 and 1916; the only hits were EO 1547 itself, EO 2514 (January 15, 1917, Canal Zone leave rules, effective December 31, 1916) and EO 4459 (1926, Canal overtime pay), none of which names this waiver or acts before 1915. A citation search of every held order text for 'No. 1547' or 'Order 1547' found only Proclamation No. 1547 of 1919 (Scotts Bluff), a different instrument. The date is a fixed term of the waiver, not a deadline on another act.

independent_command_check: No independent command survives. The recital of section 2 of the 1912 act is authority, not a command. The waiver has no proviso imposing a separate continuing duty.

Under the March 4, 1917 naval appropriation act proviso it orders that 'during the present national emergency' the eight-hour limit is suspended for contracts for miscellaneous changes at the Barge Office, New York City, to accommodate the Customs Intelligence Bureau under the act of July 1, 1918, with overtime computed under the 1917 act. Its own terms tie it to the emergency; it ends at the earlier of the contracts' completion and the end of the 'present national emergency'.

research_rationale: EO 4782 (December 16, 1927, Calvin Coolidge), read in full in the held ProQuest replica scan (archival_replica_scan_pending_codebook, acceptable_as_original false) and checked against the page image I rendered from the held PDF (sha256 cf42ef50...; one page; printed 'No. 4782', date 'December 16, 1927', signature 'Calvin Coolidge'; handwritten marginal note 'Holidays'). The OCR layer is complete; its trailing noise ('[No. 47821', 'Trlu', '97f') is the printed number and the handwritten note, not order text. It closes the executive departments and independent establishments in the District of Columbia, including the Government Printing Office and the Navy Yard and stations, on Saturday, December 24, 1927, and excuses federal employees in the District from duty that day, except those excepted for special public reasons or whose absence would conflict with existing law. Its last sentence says 'This Order is not to be deemed as establishing a precedent.' The type label closing_mourning fits. First end: by its own terms at the close of 1927-12-24, the only day it governs. A reader who dates cessation to the first day without effect would write 1927-12-25; this claim records 1927-12-24, the day through whose end the order ran, consistent with the owner's inclusive reading of stated dates. The census register gives only the year; the date December 16, 1927 comes from the scan and agrees with the WPA 1944 list ('1928 CSR 78').

Searches on 2026-10-28: census titles and type rows for 1927-1928 closings; the WPA 1944 numbered list for Christmas or December 24 closings in 1927 and 1928; and a citation search of every held order text for 'No. 4782' or 'Order 4782'. The only related order found is EO 5008 (1928), which closes the same offices on December 24, 1928; it is a new one-day order, not an extension or amendment of EO 4782, and does not name it. Nothing names EO 4782. The machine USC and eCFR searches (complete, 0 hits) exclude a current-law reference; the OFR catalog search starts in 1937 and is not relied on alone.
scope_check: Whole order is one clause governing one day. No partial event is held or found.
independent_command_check: The closing and the excusal from duty are one command for one day. The sentence 'This Order is not to be deemed as establishing a precedent' commands no one; it limits how the order may be read and has no operation once the day has passed, so it is not a retained independent command.

research_rationale: EO 6874 (October 16, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription. It is not a closing order: under the Civil Service Act of January 16, 1883 it amends paragraph 6 of subdivision VII of schedule A of the civil-service rules 'to read as follows': '6. Temporary clerks, carriers, and laborers required for part-time or intermittent work in the Postal Service in connection with the present holiday or seasonal business from this date to February 1, 1935.' The type label closing_mourning is wrong; the WPA 1944 list (1935 CSR 28) and the APP title agree that it is a Schedule A amendment. Most probable reading: the exception it inserted ran by its own terms from October 16, 1934 to February 1, 1935 (inclusive reading; exclusive alternative ends at the start of that day). The WPA list shows no further amendment of Subdivision VII paragraph 6 between October 16, 1934 and February 1, 1935; EO 7209 (October 19, 1935; held as jobs/hathi-gpo-orders/output/texts/EO_7209.txt) later rewrote paragraph 6 'from this date to February 1, 1936'.
